This appeal is filed by the owners and driver of the offending vehicle i.e. Tractor No. C.G. - 08 - C - 8699 And Tractor Trolley No. C.G. - 07 - 1158 challenging the impugned award dated 25.04.2019 passed by the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bemetara, District - Bemetara (C.G.) in Claim Case No. 126/2017 whereby, the learned Claims Tribunal has awarded Rs. 6,46,000/- as amount of compensation to the respondents in a fatal accident case and fastened liability upon Non- Applicants No. 1 to 3 to satisfy the award.

entities.text: Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Bemetara, District - Bemetara

sentences.text: 2. Facts of the case in brief are that, on 08.03.2009, after loading bricks in the offending vehicle Tractor bearing registration no. C.G. - 08 - C - 8699, the deceased namely Gautriha along with the other labourers was going towards Manpur from Village Patarjhori.

The offending vehicle was driven by the Non-applicant No. 1/Appellant No. 1 herein , reached near a bridge in Village Manpur,
due to rash and negligent driving of the Non-applicant No. 1, the deceased namely, Gautriha fell down from the vehicle and sustained grievous injuries.

He was taken to hospital on the same tractor,
but he succumbed to his injuries.

Subsequent to the said incident, F.I.R. bearing Crime No. 47/2009 at P.S. Gandai, District - Rajnandgaon was registered against the Non- Applicant No. 4.
3.

Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the Claims Tribunal erred in fastening liability upon the driver and owners of the Tractor and Trolley (Appellants No. 1 to 3) overlooking the fact that on the date of accident, the driver of the offending Tractor was possessed with valid and effective driving license.

He contended that the learned Claims Tribunal erroneously recorded a finding that there was breach of conditions of the insurance policy which is without there being any cogent and reliable piece of evidence.
4. I have heard learned counsel for the appellant and perused the record of claim case.

5. The claimants in the claim application have specifically pleaded that the deceased at the time of accident was traveling on Tractor Engine and sitting by the side of driver, due to rash and negligent driving of the offending Tractor by the Non-Applicant No. 1/Driver, deceased Gautriha fell down suffered severe injuries and later on, succumbed to the injuries.
In reply to the claim application, the Appellants/Non-Applicants No. 1 to 3 have admitted the fact of falling of Gautriha from the Tractor Engine while driving it.
However, they have pleaded that the deceased fell down from the offending Tractor Engine because of his own negligence.
6. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case of New India Assurance Company Ltd. Vs. Vedwati & Ors.

On an erroneous impression this Court came to the conclusion that the insurer would be liable to pay compensation in respect of the death or bodily injury caused to either the owner of the goods or his authorised representative when being carried in a goods vehicle the accident occurred.

If the Motor Vehicles Amendment Act of 1994 is examined, particularly Section 46, by which the expression "injury to any person" in the original Act stood substituted by the expression "injury to any person including owner of the goods or his authorised representative carried in the vehicle", the conclusion is irresistible that prior to the aforesaid Amendment Act of 1994, even if the widest interpretation is given to the expression "to any person" it will not cover either the owner of the goods or his authorised representative being carried in the vehicle.

Francis Bennion in his book Statutory Interpretation described 'purposive interpretation' as under:
'A purposive construction of an enactment is one which gives effect to the legislative purpose by- (a) following the literal meaning of the enactment where that meaning is in accordance with the legislative purpose, or (b) applying a stained meaning where the literal meaning is not in accordance with the legislative purpose.' 35[38].
More often than not, literal interpretation of a statute or a provision of a statute results in absurdity.
Therefore, while interpreting statutory provisions, the courts should keep in mind the objectives or purpose for which statute has been enacted.

Justice Frankfurter of US Supreme Court in an article titled as 'Some Reflections on the reading of Statutes' ( 47 Columbia Law Review 527),
observed that, ' legislation has an aim, it seeks to obviate some mischief, to supply an adequacy, to effect a change of policy, to formulate a plan of Government.

10. From the aforementioned facts and decisions, it is undisputed that at the time of accident, the deceased Gautriha was traveling on the Tractor Engine.
There is no sitting capacity on the Tractor Engine except the driver of the Tractor.
Copy of the insurance policy of the Tractor is filed as NA - 1C.
Perusal of the policy would show that the premium is paid for accidental benefits.
Under the head of personal accident for owner and driver, for paid driver and risk of any other person is not covered under the policy.
The Non-applicant No. 4/Insurance Company has examined Praveen Sijariya as NAW -1.
He proved the policy to be issued by the respondent.
In his evidence, he has not specifically stated that the vehicle was insured for agricultural purpose.

This witness was cross-examined by the company on behalf of the claimants, however, no suggestion was given with regard to the purpose of the insurance of the vehicle for agricultural purposes only is perverse to the contents of the policy.
In the facts of the case, the evidence brought on record by the insurance company is accepted.

11. Learned Claims Tribunal has recorded a finding that on the date of accident, the vehicle was being used for carrying bricks and there is no suggestive piece of evidence that the bricks were being transported for some work relating to agricultural activities.

In the aforementioned facts of the case,
the finding recorded by the learned Claims Tribunal that on the date of accident, the offending vehicle is being used for other than the agricultural purposes which cannot be said to be erroneous.

Further, as per the pleadings made by the claimants and the Appellants/Non-applicants No. 1 to 3, it is proved that at the time of accident, deceased was traveling on the Tractor Engine and fell down from it and succumbed to his injuries and thereby, there was breach of policy conditions.
12. In view of the aforementioned evidence available on record, I do not find any perversity or illegality in the award passed by the learned Claims Tribunal.
The appeal being sans merit is liable to be and accordingly, dismissed.
